Pick any subset of any topological space, apply **closure** and **complement** in every order you like, and you will never generate more than 14 distinct sets. [Kuratowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuratowski%27s_closure-complement_problem) proved this astounding fact in 1922.

Most subsets fall well short of that bound. Reaching exactly 14 demands a starting set where every operation breaks new ground. The canonical choice on $\mathbb{R}$ is:

$$A = (0,1) \cup (1,2) \cup \{3\} \cup \bigl([4,5] \cap \mathbb{Q}\bigr)$$

**Each piece does specific topological work:**

- **$(0,1) \cup (1,2)$** --- two open intervals separated by a missing point at $1$; closure fills it.
- **$\{3\}$** --- an isolated point; complement erases it, closure keeps it.
- **$[4,5] \cap \mathbb{Q}$** --- rationals dense in $[4,5]$; closure fills in the irrationals, but complement exposes them.

The chart traces the full orbit of $A$ — and the pattern only becomes clear when you see them all at once.
